134.title: Rehras at dusk
134.hook: the evening prayer, said as the day's work ends
134.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib at sunset, at home or in the gurdwara, as the evening part of Nitnem; it opens with So Dar and includes Chaupai and part of Anand Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand Sahib, the song of bliss. Your line was joy, found. Who did you tell your good news to? We've finished the morning. Now the light starts to go. Day one hundred thirty-four.

There's a particular moment at the end of a workday. You shut the laptop, or clock out, or take off your boots at the door. The bag hits the floor. For a second, you're between things: the day's not quite over, the evening hasn't started. It's easy to fill that second with the phone, the news, the next chore. In Sikh practice, that moment belongs to something else. As the sun goes down, someone lights a lamp, or just sits, and the evening prayer begins. Today, Rehras.
screen: `THE BAG HITS THE FLOOR.` → `BETWEEN DAY AND EVENING.` → `THE EVENING PRAYER BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Rehras Sahib is the Sikh evening bani, said around sunset, as the day's work ends. It's a collection rather than a single hymn: hymns from the Gurus in the Guru Granth Sahib, and then Chaupai, part of Anand Sahib, and a few closing verses. So some of it you've already met this week. It opens with a hymn called So Dar, that door. It's a version of a passage from Japji, and it asks a huge, open question. In paraphrase: what is that door, and what is that home, where you sit and care for all? Then it answers with music. Countless instruments are playing there, countless singers in countless ragas are singing your praise: wind, water and fire sing, the continents and the worlds sing. At the end of a long day, when your world has shrunk to your inbox and your sore feet, Rehras opens the window as wide as it goes. Where does the name come from? Readers explain it more than one way. Some connect it to a word for supplication, a humble petition. Others hear rah, a road, and read it as provisions for the journey. Both readings fit. It's a pause for the traveler, at the point where the day's road runs out. And the hymns of Rehras return the day to the hukam, the Divine Order, that sustains it all. Said at sunset, they can be heard as a way of handing the day back: what you did, what was done to you, set down inside something larger before the night.
screen: `AT SUNSET, AS WORK ENDS.` · `SO DAR — WHAT IS THAT DOOR?` · `THE WHOLE WORLD SINGING.` · `PROVISIONS FOR THE ROAD.` · then, large: `PUT THE DAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: Stop for two minutes, as if it were dusk. If it's not evening where you are, pretend. Sit down and let your hands rest in your lap. Think of three things from today, or yesterday: one thing you did, one thing that happened to you, one thing still unfinished. As you breathe out, picture setting each one down on a table beside you. Not solving them. Just putting them down. If you pray, you can hand them over. The bell holds the time.
Rehras. The Sikh evening prayer, said at sunset as work ends, opening with So Dar: what is that door?
Your line: put the day down. This evening, when the light goes, take two minutes before the phone and set the day down, one thing at a time. Day one hundred thirty-four.

135.title: Kirtan Sohila at night
135.hook: five short hymns said before sleep
135.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila at night before sleep as the last bani of Nitnem; it is also read at funerals after cremation, and when the Guru Granth Sahib is closed for the night in the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rehras at dusk. Your line was put the day down. Did you manage two minutes at sunset before the phone won? Tonight, the last door of the day. Day one hundred thirty-five.

What's the last thing you do before you fall asleep? For a lot of us, honestly, it's the phone: one more scroll, one more video, the blue light on the ceiling. Then we wonder why sleep is thin. Parents know a better way from the other side. A child's bedtime has a ritual: the bath, the story, the song, the light going off. The same song every night, so the child knows it's safe to let go. Sikhs have a bedtime song of their own. Today, Kirtan Sohila.
screen: `ONE MORE SCROLL.` → `A CHILD'S BEDTIME SONG.` → `THE SIKH NIGHT SONG.`

segments.voice: Kirtan Sohila is short: five hymns, in the Guru Granth Sahib. Three are by Guru Nanak, one by Guru Ram Das, one by Guru Arjan. It's the last bani of the Sikh day, said at night before sleep. Sohila means a song of praise, and in Punjab it's also a word for the songs sung at weddings. That's a clue. The first hymn, by Guru Nanak, uses wedding pictures. In paraphrase: in the house where the Creator's praises are sung, sing the song of praise and remember the Creator. Then it speaks of a bride whose wedding day has been set, and of friends pouring oil on the threshold, the old custom for welcoming a bride, and asks them to bless her so she may meet her Lord. The bride is the soul. The wedding is the meeting with God. And here's what makes Sohila unusual: that wedding also means death. Sikhs read Kirtan Sohila not only every night but at funerals, after a cremation. The same song for sleep and for death. That can sound grim, but it isn't meant that way. Sleep is a small letting go every night. The Gurus picture death, the great letting go, as a wedding day, not a door slamming. Saying Sohila at night rehearses trust: whatever the night holds, the soul is not going somewhere cold. Another hymn in Sohila, one of Guru Nanak's, describes the whole sky as a platter for God's worship: sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls. You're lying down under that sky tonight.

Close your eyes and picture your bedroom tonight, the phone already face down across the room. Picture the lights off and the sky outside your window: moon, stars. If you pray, imagine the first line of Sohila there. If not, just picture yourself letting go, the way a child does when the song ends. The bell holds the time.
Sohila. A song of praise, and a wedding song: five hymns Sikhs say at night, and at funerals too.
Your line: the night song. Tonight, let the last thing before sleep be one minute of Kirtan Sohila, or one minute of quiet, not the scroll. Day one hundred thirty-five.

136.title: How long it takes
136.hook: the full Nitnem takes an hour or more, and traditions differ slightly on which banis are included
136.howItsDone: A full Nitnem takes an hour or more each day; Sikhs who have taken amrit keep it as part of their vows, while many others and newcomers begin with one bani, such as Japji or Sohila, and add more over time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kirtan Sohila, the bedtime song. Your line was the night song. Did Sohila, or a minute of quiet, beat the scroll last night? Day one hundred thirty-six.

Let's do the math honestly, the way you'd look at a recipe before you start cooking. You've now met all the Nitnem banis: Japji, Jaap, the savaiyas, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras, Sohila. That's a lot of words, spread from before breakfast to just before sleep. So what does a full day of Nitnem actually take? And is everyone doing exactly the same thing? Two plain questions, with two plain answers, and neither of them is meant to scare anyone off.
screen: `READ THE RECIPE FIRST.` → `SEVEN BANIS SO FAR.` → `WHAT DOES IT REALLY TAKE?`

segments.voice: First, the time. The morning banis are the long part: Japji, Jaap, the savaiyas, Chaupai and all of Anand, read at a steady pace, fill most of the hour. Someone who has said them every day for years goes faster. Rehras in the evening is shorter. Kirtan Sohila at night takes only a few minutes. So a full Nitnem is an hour or more across the day. Second, the differences. Sikhs share the core, but not every detail is the same everywhere. The Rehat Maryada from the Akal Takht lists three morning banis; other Sikhs, especially those who have taken amrit, say five. Some traditions, like the Damdami Taksal and some jathas, recite a longer Rehras or a longer Chaupai. Some Sikhs add more banis on top, like Sukhmani or Asa di Var in the morning. These are differences of practice within one faith, not a ranking of who prays properly. Third, the most useful thing. Sikhs who have taken amrit commit to Nitnem as part of their vows. For many others, and certainly for learners, it's normal to grow into it. A child might learn the Mul Mantar first, then Japji's first pauri, then more. An adult coming back to the faith might begin with Japji alone, or Sohila at night. Nobody arrives at the full hour on day one. Nitnem means the daily rule, and its weight is on daily. One bani, said every day, becomes a path worn across a field.
screen: `AN HOUR OR MORE A DAY.` · `THE CORE, AND THE DIFFERENCES.` · `A VOW FOR SOME, A ROAD FOR OTHERS.` · `STEADINESS OVER SIZE.` · then, large: `START WITH ONE.`

segments.voice: Pick one bani to begin with. Close your eyes, and don't run through a list. Wait a moment and see which one comes back on its own: a line, a tune, a picture. Don't pick the one you think you should. Pick the one that comes back. Hold it in mind now, and breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
How long it takes. A full Nitnem is an hour or more a day, with small differences between traditions, and many grow into it one bani at a time.
Your line: start with one. Today, find the bani you picked, in a gutka, an app or a recording, and save it where you'll see it tomorrow. Day one hundred thirty-six.

137.title: Your Nitnem, for now
137.hook: a starter Nitnem is an invitation, not a test
137.howItsDone: Amritdhari Sikhs keep the full Nitnem as part of their vows; many other Sikhs and newcomers begin with one bani said daily, such as Japji in the morning or Sohila at night, and add more over time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how long it takes: an hour or more, and small differences between traditions. Your line was start with one. Did you save the bani you picked? Day one hundred thirty-seven.
screen: `HOW LONG IT TAKES — START WITH ONE.`

segments.voice: Two pieces of paper land on a desk. One is a test, face down, with a box for a grade. The other is a card with a name written on the envelope. A daily prayer can look like the first: a full version you either pass or fail, so why start? Today we finish our ten days on Nitnem, and the point of the day is the second piece of paper. A starter Nitnem is closer to an invitation than a test.
screen: `THE PAPER, FACE DOWN.` → `PASS OR FAIL?` → `AN INVITATION, NOT A TEST.`

segments.voice: Look at where we've been. Nitnem: the daily discipline, morning, evening, night. Japji at dawn, where Guru Nanak says clever thinking won't get you there. Jaap Sahib, galloping praise of the Timeless. The savaiyas: without love, nothing. Chaupai: keep me. Anand: joy, found. Rehras at dusk: put the day down. Sohila at night: the song for sleep. And yesterday, the honest math. So what's a Nitnem for now? For Sikhs who have taken amrit, the full Nitnem is part of their vows, and they keep it. For everyone else walking this path, whether you're a Sikh coming back to practice, someone learning alongside a Sikh partner, or simply curious, the Gurus' own words point to a gentler start. Gurbani often calls the Guru's word amrit, nectar: something offered to drink. And the Granth's very first lines, the Mul Mantar, end with two words: gur prasad, by the Guru's grace. In that reading, the invitation isn't earned. It's given. So a starter Nitnem might be Japji's first pauri each morning. Or Sohila at night. Or Anand's first stanza with your coffee. Whatever it is, it's said daily, at a time that already exists in your day. And when a day slips, you do what we learned on the breath. You come back.

138.title: Before you go
138.hook: anyone is welcome; cover your head, take off your shoes, bring no tobacco or alcohol
138.howItsDone: Visitors of any faith are welcome in a gurdwara; they cover their heads, remove their shoes, wash their hands, bring no tobacco or alcohol, and sit on the floor in the main hall.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your Nitnem, for now. Your line was one bani, daily. Did you say or play the one you chose this morning? Now we step out of the house, to a new stretch: the gurdwara. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

Where do I stand? What do I touch? What if I do something wrong and everybody notices? Those are the questions of anyone stepping into a stranger's kitchen, or a stranger's place of prayer. A gurdwara can be driven past for years by someone curious who never goes in, because nobody told them the rules. So before the next week of visiting, here's the simple part: what to know before you go. And the first thing to know comes first for a reason. You're allowed in.
screen: `A STRANGER'S KITCHEN.` → `WHAT IF I GET IT WRONG?` → `YOU'RE ALLOWED IN.`

segments.voice: Gurdwara means the door of the Guru, or the Guru's gateway. It's the Sikh place of worship, and its doors are open to everyone: Sikhs, people of any other faith, people of none. That openness is written into Sikh history. The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the Golden Temple, was built with entrances on all four sides, and Sikhs read that as a sign that people from every direction and every background are welcome. It's also set lower than the ground around it, so you step down to enter, which tradition reads as humility. So what do you actually do? Just a few things, all about respect for the Guru Granth Sahib, which is present in the main hall. Cover your head. Men, women and children all do this. A scarf, a bandana, anything that covers the hair. Gurdwaras often keep a basket of head coverings by the door if you forget. Take off your shoes. There's usually a shoe rack or a room for them, and often a place to wash your hands, and sometimes your feet. Bring no tobacco, alcohol or drugs, not even in a pocket. The Sikh code of conduct forbids tobacco and intoxicants, and they don't come into the gurdwara. Dress modestly, and expect to sit on the floor. That's it. Nobody will ask what you believe. Nobody will ask you to join anything. If you're unsure what to do next, ask, and someone will usually show you, often with a plate of food to follow. Hospitality is part of what a gurdwara is for.
screen: `GURDWARA — THE GURU'S DOOR.` · `FOUR DOORS, EVERY DIRECTION.` · `HEAD COVERED, SHOES OFF.` · `NO TOBACCO, NO ALCOHOL.` · then, large: `EVERYONE IS WELCOME.`

segments.voice: Find your nearest gurdwara. If you have a map app, search for gurdwara now and see how far the closest one is. The bell holds the time.

Your line: everyone is welcome. Today, find one place where you could make someone else feel welcome, and do it the gurdwara's way, with a smile and something to eat. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

139.title: The flag outside
139.hook: a tall saffron flag bearing the khanda marks a gurdwara from far away
139.howItsDone: A Nishan Sahib, a saffron or blue flag bearing the khanda on a cloth-wrapped pole, stands outside every gurdwara; its cloth is often renewed each year at Vaisakhi, and some Sikhs bow toward it on arrival.

segments.voice: Yesterday, before you go: head covered, shoes off, no tobacco or alcohol. Your line was everyone is welcome. Did you find your nearest gurdwara? Today, how you'd spot it from the road. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

A traveler on a Punjab road, long ago. It's getting dark, the road is dusty, and she's hungry, with nowhere to stay. Then, above the rooftops of the next village, she sees it: a tall pole, and at the top a triangle of saffron cloth moving in the wind. She doesn't need to ask anyone. She knows what it means. There will be food there, and a place to sleep, and nobody will ask who she is. You can still see that same sign today, in Amritsar, in California, in the suburbs of London.
screen: `A TRAVELER AT DUSK.` → `SAFFRON ABOVE THE ROOFS.` → `SHE KNOWS WHAT IT MEANS.`

segments.voice: It's called the Nishan Sahib. Nishan means a sign, a mark, a flag; sahib is the word of respect. The Sikh code of conduct asks for one at every gurdwara: a tall flagpole, usually wrapped in cloth of the same color, with a flag that is most often saffron, and sometimes a deep blue. On the flag is the khanda, the Sikh emblem. Look closely and it's made of three shapes. In the middle, a double-edged sword, also called a khanda. Around it, a circle, the chakkar, which has no beginning and no end. And on either side, two curved swords, often explained as spiritual and worldly responsibility held together. At the top of the pole there's usually a steel khanda too. Sikh tradition credits the sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, with raising a flag at the Akal Takht in Amritsar. What does it say? It says: a gurdwara is here. And in practice a gurdwara means more than prayer. It means langar, the free kitchen, and a place for a traveler to rest. So the flag is a promise made in public, to anyone who can see it. Sikhs treat the Nishan Sahib with care. In many gurdwaras the cloth is taken down and replaced each year, often at Vaisakhi, and the pole is washed, sometimes with milk and water, in a small ceremony with prayers. And some Sikhs bow toward the flag as they arrive, before they even reach the door.

Either way, spend these two minutes with the khanda: close your eyes and picture it. The sword in the middle. The circle with no end. The two curved swords on either side. Hold the shape still in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Nishan Sahib. The tall flag outside a gurdwara, saffron or blue, bearing the khanda: a sign that says come in.

Your line: the flag says come in. Today, think about what your own front door says to people. Then make one thing say come in: a message, a porch light, a chair pulled out. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

segments.voice: You've left your shoes at the rack. Your head is covered. You step into the main hall, the darbar, and it's bigger and brighter than you expected. Carpets, or white sheets, cover the floor. People sit cross-legged. Music is playing: harmonium, tabla, voices singing. And at the far end, raised up under a canopy, wrapped in beautiful cloth, is a book. One by one, people walk up the middle of the room toward it, kneel, and touch their foreheads to the floor. What are they doing, and what are they bowing to?
screen: `THE DARBAR, BRIGHT AND OPEN.` → `A BOOK UNDER A CANOPY.` → `FOREHEADS TO THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: It's called matha tekna. Matha is the forehead. Tekna means to rest, to lean it down. So it's resting your forehead before the Guru. And the Guru here is the Guru Granth Sahib. Sikh tradition tells that in 1708, before he died, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, declared there would be no more human Gurus after him. The Guru would be the word itself, the scripture, alongside the community, the Khalsa Panth. So when Sikhs bow in the gurdwara, they're not bowing to paper and ink, and not to an idol. They're bowing to the Guru's word, the living teacher, present in the room. How it's done: people walk slowly up the central aisle, often with hands folded. Many place an offering in front of the Granth, some money in the box called the golak, or food for the langar kitchen, or nothing at all. Then they kneel and touch their forehead to the floor. Afterward they step back and sit down among the sangat, usually taking care not to sit with their feet or back pointing toward the Guru Granth Sahib. The offering isn't a fee. The gurdwara runs on the community's giving, and the golak pays for the langar and the building, but nobody checks what you gave. Visitors aren't required to bow. Many do, as a sign of respect, the way you'd stand when someone honored walks into a room. Others simply sit quietly, and that's fine too. The point is the humility. The head, which we spend all day raising, goes down, before a word bigger than we are.
screen: `MATHA — FOREHEAD. TEKNA — TO REST.` · `1708: THE WORD BECOMES GURU.` · `THE AISLE, THE GOLAK, THE BOW.` · `THE HEAD GOES DOWN.` · then, large: `BOW TO THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Bow once, wherever you are. If you're able, kneel and rest your forehead on the floor, or on your folded hands, or on a table in front of you. If kneeling isn't possible, just lower your head. Stay there for a few breaths. Notice what it feels like to put the head, the busiest part of you, lower than your heart. If you pray, you can bow to the Guru's word. If not, bow to whatever you owe gratitude today. Then sit up slowly. The bell holds the time.
Matha tekna. Resting the forehead to the floor before the Guru Granth Sahib: bowing to the word, not to paper.
Your line: bow to the word. Today, when you read something wise, a line, a verse, a sentence from someone you trust, pause and lower your head for one breath. Day one hundred forty.
